title: An inexact sequential quadratic optimization algorithm for nonlinear optimization
contribution: An SQP method with an l1 exact penalty that accepts inexact primal-dual QP solutions satisfying four loose termination tests and six scenarios, proves well-posedness and global convergence to KKT, infeasible stationary or MFCQ-failing FJ points, and shows on 309 CUTE problems (with emulated inexactness) about the same reliability and close iteration counts as exact QP solves (pp. 9-12, 27, 29-31).
problem_entry: Classical SQO needs exact QP solves; asks for the loosest per-iteration accuracy test that keeps global convergence and the automatic transition to the feasibility problem of the authors' own exact two-QP method [5], which required exact solves (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Exact Algorithm A (PQP plus FQP reference, Scenarios A-C with steering-like convex combination and penalty update) as scaffold; iSQO replaces exact solves by residual-ratio, multiplier-bound and model-reduction tests checked inside the QP solver, adding null-primal-step Scenarios 1, 5, 6 so that an exact solve is never needed (pp. 5-14).
assumptions: f, c, cbar C1 with bounded Lipschitz first derivatives on a convex set containing iterates; bounded Hessian approximations; QP solver assumed to drive the residual to zero with objective no worse than d = 0 (Assumptions 3.1-3.3, 3.15-3.16, pp. 14-15, 19); MFCQ only in outcome classification; no local rate analysis.
proof_devices: well-posedness chain: finite convexification (Lemma 3.4), reachability of each termination test (Lemmas 3.5, 3.7, 3.8), finite inner termination (Lemma 3.9), exactly one scenario occurs defining index sets K_i (Lemma 3.10) (pp. 15-18)
-Delta l_k as surrogate for the directional derivative of the l1 penalty function (Lemma 3.12, cited to Burke) and model-reduction lower bounds after the penalty update (Lemma 3.13) (pp. 18-19)
step-size lower bound alpha_k >= omega * Delta l_k from Taylor plus convexity of the 1-norm (Lemma 3.18, p. 20)
shifted penalty phi = mu (f - f_low) + v monotone across penalty decreases (Lemma 3.19, p. 21)

generic sequence lemma: r_{k+1} <= kappa r_k + e_k on infinite K and <= max{r_k, rbar_k} elsewhere implies r_k -> 0 (Lemma 3.21, pp. 21-22), used for feasibility and penalty residuals (Lemmas 3.22-3.23, pp. 22-26)

outcome classification when mu -> 0: limit points all feasible or all infeasible (Lemma 3.24, p. 26); nonzero multipliers at feasible FJ point imply MFCQ fails (Lemma 3.28, p. 27); Theorem 3.29 and Corollary 3.30 (pp. 27-28)
test conditions designed backwards from the proof: Test 2 (a),(b) and (2.27) exist so that mu -> 0 with v -> 0 forces MFCQ failure (p. 10)
experiments: Matlab prototype; inexactness emulated by perturbing exact bqpd solutions by 0.5^j u until a test holds, exact solution in same code as comparator; Ipopt scaling; presolve off; 309 CUTE AMPL problems filtered by size and by bqpd not failing in any variant; exit counts (~96% success, Table 2), binned accepted residual ratios (Table 3), log2 outperforming factor of iterations ordered by size (Fig. 1); no CPU time (pp. 28-31).
positioning: Extends authors' inexact Newton SQP/IPM line [7, 8, 13-15] and Burke-Curtis-Wang two-QP SQP [5] (which needed exact QP solves) to inequalities; cites inexact Newton [16, 42], inexact constrained Newton [29, 31, 37, 41], l1 penalty SQO, steering [5, 9, 11, 12, 22]; scopes out inexact-derivative SQO; no rival code compared (pp. 2, 7).
writing: Novelty sentence in abstract, introduction and conclusion; exact algorithm explicitly presented 'as motivation and for reference'; each test followed by its purpose and the lemma needing it; heavy hedging in numerics ('preliminary', 'suggest', 'may') (pp. 1, 8-12, 28, 31-32).
limits_future: Inexactness simulated, no iterative QP solver or timing; does not reduce exactly to Algorithm A; no local convergence; future: real-time optimal control with hot-started QPs and cheap Jacobian products, and large-scale problems with fast inexact QP solvers (pp. 8, 28-29, 32).

method_links.note: QP termination tests derived from l1-penalty model reduction and residual ratios the outer method needs, checked inside the QP solver, with convexification also moved inside; also Heuristic 10: exact twin Algorithm A built first, only exact QP solves replaced
Steps 4-6 not done: no relative-residual baselines, no production integration or timing; inexactness emulated by perturbing exact bqpd solutions because no suitable QP solver existed
single algorithm automatically transitions to minimizing l1 infeasibility; penalty update via convex combination with FQP reference step and model-reduction tests (Scenario C/4)

comparator differs only in inner-solve accuracy (unperturbed exact solution in same code); Ipopt problem scaling adopted. Heuristic 7 variant: test set excludes problems where bqpd failed in any variant, no pre-filter count

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: each iteration falls in exactly one named scenario with conditions and updates; Lemma 3.10 proves exhaustiveness; analysis runs over index sets K_i
exact bqpd solutions perturbed by 0.5^j random vectors until a termination test is just met, to test the theory's tests before an inner solver supports them
implemented infeasibility exit additionally requires mu_k <= mu_low, unlike Algorithm 2, with the reason stated

transferable: Design the inexact method as exact algorithm plus extra scenarios that make an exact solve never necessary, and say which scenarios would be vacuous under exact solves (pp. 8, 12).
Use the 'contract on an infinite subsequence, don't grow elsewhere' sequence lemma for residuals reduced only by some iteration types (Lemma 3.21, pp. 21-22).
Shifted penalty function mu (f - f_low) + v whose monotonicity survives penalty decreases (Lemma 3.19, p. 21).
Require a small penalty parameter in the infeasibility exit test so the code does not stop early on problems it could still solve (pp. 28-29).
Emulate inexact inner solves by perturbing exact solutions until the test is just satisfied, running the exact solution in the same code as comparator (p. 29).
Report binned per-problem minimum and geometric-mean accepted residual ratios to show the inexactness was real (Table 3, p. 30).
Plot log2 iteration ratios ordered by problem size to check whether inexactness hurts more on larger problems (pp. 30-31).
coauthors: Travis C. Johnson, Daniel P. Robinson, Andreas Waechter

quotes.text: In this manner, the QP solver iterates until the needs of the (outer) algorithm are met.
We disabled the AMPL presolve feature to maintain the idiosyncrasies of each formulation.

title: A quasi-Newton algorithm for nonconvex, nonsmooth optimization with global convergence guarantees
contribution: A BFGS-gradient-sampling hybrid for locally Lipschitz nonconvex nonsmooth minimization that behaves as plain BFGS in most iterations, adds adaptive gradient sampling and a bounded L-BFGS fallback when monitored tests fail, is proved globally convergent with probability one, and is implemented in C++ and benchmarked against HANSO and LMBM with an independent stationarity measure (pp. 2, 7-15, 20-28).
problem_entry: Practitioners see BFGS work on nonsmooth problems but its guarantees are limited [35]; named defects: no stationarity-based termination and inverse Hessians tending to singularity; GS has guarantees but costly iterations without curvature (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Direction d = -W G y from the dual of a sampled-gradient piecewise-quadratic model (reduces to BFGS with one sample); radius reduced only under stationarity, curvature and positive-step tests; truncated Armijo-Wolfe search, iterate perturbation into D, sample-set reset or random growth, damped BFGS in good iterations and bounded damped L-BFGS otherwise (pp. 5-14).
assumptions: f locally Lipschitz, C1 on open dense D (Assumption 2.1, p. 4); Clarke epsilon-stationarity; curvature threshold xi bounded by (3.1) (p. 15), which the implementation violates, and D membership not checked in code (p. 20); Lemma 2.4 needs weak lower semismoothness, which the authors decline to assume (p. 10).
proof_devices: dual-QP identity ||G y||_W = ||d||_{W^-1} and strict descent (Lemma 2.2, p. 7)
eigenvalue bounds for damped, update-skipping L-BFGS by induction over m updates (Lemmas 2.7-2.8, pp. 13-14)
infinitely many positive steps by contradiction with sample-set growth (Lemma 3.3, p. 16)
approximate least W-norm element lemma (Lemma 3.5, p. 16) and existence of good sample sets near a limit point (Lemma 3.6, cited to [14, 32], p. 17)

Case 1/Case 2 split; Case 2: bounded L-BFGS makes curvature test always hold, iterates Cauchy, and both subcases (limit epsilon-stationary or not) shown to be probability-zero events via fresh resampling and Lebourg's mean value theorem (pp. 17-19)
final step epsilon_k -> 0 implies stationary cluster points taken verbatim from [14, Theorem 4.2, Case 2] (p. 19)
experiments: C++ bfgs-gs vs hanso-bfgs, hanso-default, lmbm at defaults with iteration limits on par; 26 scalable problems, n = 50 (64), 10 starts each = 260 runs; CPU ignored (language differences), iterations/function/gradient evaluations; termination-flag counts (Table 4); profiles count all runs successful; independent epsilon-stationarity from 10^3 fresh random points in a 10^-2 ball, geometric means (Table 5); own code at two tolerances; own parameters chosen as 'worked well in our tests'; losses on problem 20 and others printed (pp. 20-28).
positioning: Builds on Lewis-Overton BFGS for nonsmooth [35], Burke-Lewis-Overton GS [7] and Curtis-Que adaptive GS [14]; separates GS from bundle methods (no cutting planes); describes HANSO as BFGS-then-GS switch with similar guarantees and plain BFGS as having guarantees only for simple problems (pp. 2-3, 21).
writing: Design intent stated as a feature ('This feature is intentional'); motivation before each algorithm box; methodological caveats (flags, CPU, random points) argued in main text; results framed as 'versatility' and 'competitive with-and in some ways outperforms' (pp. 2, 8-12, 24-28).
limits_future: Guarantees rely on bounded L-BFGS fallback; implementation violates xi bound; poor runs on problem 20; tuning effort unreported; future variant letting xi and mu thresholds vary with the sampling radius not pursued because no benefit was seen (pp. 20-21, 28).

method_links.note: termination flags explicitly not trusted because flag-based success would favour the authors' code; quality judged by an algorithm-independent epsilon-stationarity estimate from fresh random samples; this is the 2015 journal source of the passage SKILL.md quotes from the Que thesis 2016. Also Heuristic 5 (fast guarantee-free BFGS kept as comparator hanso-bfgs, guarantees restored) and Heuristic 6 (CPU time ignored, iterations and evaluations reported, p. 24)
10 starts per problem with geometric means; iteration limits on par; losses printed (problem 20; Table 5 problems 6, 20, 22-24)
rivals at defaults while own parameters chosen on the evaluation set ('worked well in our tests'), tuning effort not reported (same pattern as 03 PE13)
nonsmooth analogue: one algorithm adding sampling inside BFGS iterations when monitored tests fail, contrasted with hanso-default's BFGS-then-GS switch; no penalty parameter involved

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the guaranteed method reduces to unadulterated BFGS whenever the curvature and step-size tests pass; sampling and bounded L-BFGS switch on only when they fail
implementation section states that xi violates the theoretical bound (3.1) and that membership in D is never checked

transferable: Make the safeguard dormant: the guaranteed method reduces to the trusted fast method whenever monitored tests pass (pp. 2, 11).
Swap to a freshly initialized, update-skipping L-BFGS matrix only in iterations where the proof needs a bounded metric (Algorithm 5, Lemma 2.8, pp. 13-14).
Prove a radius is eventually reduced by showing the bad event must recur on infinitely many independently resampled sets, so it has probability zero (pp. 18-19).
Table termination flags by type before profiles and say why flag-based success would bias them (Table 4, p. 25).
Certify every solver's output with the same external epsilon-stationarity measure from fresh random samples around the final iterate; geometric means over repeated starts (pp. 26-27).
Bracket rivals' solution quality by running your own code at two tolerances instead of retuning the rivals (p. 24).

quotes.text: A feature critical to the practical performance of our algorithm is that, when it is applied to solve many problem instances, the algorithm reduces to an unadulterated BFGS strategy for the majority of the iterations.
if we only considered a termination flag of type (1) to be the indicator for a successful run, then the profiles would be skewed in favor of the codes that yielded such a flag most often

title: An adaptive augmented Lagrangian method for large-scale constrained optimization
contribution: A trust-region augmented Lagrangian method that decreases the penalty parameter inside each iteration until the trial step achieves a fraction of a Cauchy steering step's reduction in a Gauss-Newton violation model, keeps matrix-free compatibility, proves well-posedness and global convergence (weaker than classical AL in one case), and beats an in-house basic AL and Lancelot in iterations and gradient evaluations on CUTEr and HS problems (pp. 6-10, 32-33, 34-42).
problem_entry: AL revival rests on matrix-free solves, but poor initial penalty or multipliers waste early effort because basic AL changes the penalty only after a full AL minimization (generic Algorithm 1, line 18-21); claim narrowed to difficult or poorly scaled problems (pp. 2, 5).
key_idea: Transfer exact-penalty steering to AL: Cauchy steering step on q_v = 0.5||c + J s||^2 in radius proportional to ||F_FEAS||, trial step on the AL model in radius proportional to ||F_AL||, decrease mu inside the iteration until (3.11c) holds (allowing violation increase when within target); multipliers updated only when feasibility and stationarity targets are met; mu only decreases (pp. 6-11).
assumptions: min f s.t. c(x) = 0, l <= x <= u, f and c C2 (p. 3); iterates in a convex compact set (Assumption 3.2, p. 18), multipliers bounded via Y_j; LICQ-type full row rank on free variables for multiplier convergence (Assumption 3.3, p. 28); no guarantee of first-order limits when mu -> 0 even under MFCQ, admitted (p. 33).
proof_devices: limit lemma as mu -> 0: AL model -> feasibility model uniformly, grad L -> J^T c, AL Cauchy step -> feasibility Cauchy step via matching backtracking indices, so the steering loop terminates (Lemma 3.4, pp. 13-15; Theorem 3.6, pp. 17-18)
Gamma_k in (1, 2] and epsilon_k devices in the Cauchy routines that make the backtracking indices match (pp. 7-8, 13)
Cauchy decrease bounds with curvature constant Omega citing More [35, Thm 4.4] (Lemma 3.5, pp. 16-17)
summability of mu-weighted decreases via Dirichlet's test for monotonically vanishing mu (Lemma 3.7, pp. 18-21)

four-way case split: multiplier-update set Y finite/infinite x mu bounded away/vanishing (Lemmas 3.8, 3.9, 3.10, 3.13, pp. 21-32), with trust-region radius bounded away from zero arguments (pp. 22, 25)
projection scaling inequality ||P[x + xi v] - x|| <= xi ||P[x + v] - x|| for xi > 1 (Lemma 3.12, pp. 30-31)
three-outcome Theorem 3.14 (p. 32)
experiments: Matlab AAL-TR vs in-house BAL-TR with mostly identical components (same CG or Cplex subproblem solver and convexification) and Lancelot with aligned options; Lancelot excluded on inequality problems to isolate steering; CATENA iteration logs first (Lancelot ~79% penalty-only iterations); 91 equality CUTEr problems with every exclusion named; BAL-TR shown on par with Lancelot, AAL-TR better in iteration and gradient-evaluation profiles; final penalty tables; 64 HS inequality problems, outcome-based exclusions, hs76 on both lists; my reading of Table 3: Algorithm 4 ends with mu < 1e-2 on 51 of 91 vs 34 for Lancelot, against the text's claim (pp. 34-42).
positioning: Credits Hestenes and Powell, matrix-free AL and ADMM for the revival; 'inspired by' exact-penalty steering [7, 8, 34]; points to stabilized SQO and AL-merit methods without comparison; treats Lancelot respectfully as very mature; thanks Gould and Conn (pp. 2-3, 36, 43).
writing: Novelty sentence in abstract and conclusion; theoretical weakness stated plainly and defended by numerics; modifications that would recover theory listed with reasons for not adopting them; experimental philosophy stated as isolating one mechanism; penalty-value claims stronger than tables appear to support (pp. 1, 33-34, 40-42).
limits_future: No guarantee mu stays bounded away from zero under MFCQ; Cauchy steering may be slow on infeasible problems; weaker case (iii) result; remedies: switch to traditional AL near solutions, more accurate steering steps, parallel r_k and s_k; 'large-scale' rests on matrix-free compatibility, largest problems dropped for Matlab size (pp. 33, 38, 43).

method_links.note: penalty update as a test on model-predicted feasibility progress inside each iteration against a steering step, not after a failed AL minimization; final penalty values tabulated (step 5). Also Heuristic 8: CATENA iteration logs for Lancelot and AAL-TR before benchmarks
proposed remedy for weaker theory is to transition to a traditional AL method near solutions to inherit its guarantees (a switch), proposed not implemented
steering subproblem needs only the Cauchy decrease the convergence proof requires; both subproblems solved inexactly to remain matrix-free

rival basic AL in same framework with mostly identical components; Lancelot options aligned; Lancelot excluded where subproblem solvers differ so the steering effect stays isolated; in-house baseline calibrated against Lancelot. Heuristic 7 variant: exclusions named but HS cut on 'both did not reach tolerances' is outcome-based, hs76 on both lists
no infeasible or degenerate variants built; problems where codes reach infeasible stationary points are removed from profiles, though named with iteration counts

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: In-house incumbent calibrated to the mature code
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: BAL-TR shown to perform like Lancelot before AAL-TR is compared to BAL-TR, which differs in one component
implemented infeasibility exit requires mu <= mu_min and problem functions prescaled, both departures from Algorithm 4 stated in the implementation section

transferable: Write the incumbent as a one-page generic algorithm and point to the exact lines where effort is wasted (Algorithm 1, p. 5).
Transfer a parameter-update rule between method families by redefining feasibility progress with the target family's own model and asking only Cauchy decrease of the reference step (pp. 6-9).
Prove a parameter-reduction loop terminates by showing the subproblem model and Cauchy step converge to the feasibility ones as the parameter goes to zero (Lemma 3.4, pp. 13-15).
Use Dirichlet's test to sum mu-weighted decreases when mu decreases monotonically to zero (Lemma 3.7, p. 19).
Calibrate your reimplemented incumbent against the mature code before claiming gains, then compare against the reimplementation (pp. 34, 39).
Open experiments with one small problem's iteration log for incumbent and new method, with a column exposing the mechanism (pp. 35-38).
When your theory is weaker than the incumbent's, list the modifications that would recover it and why you did not make them (p. 33).

quotes.text: Nonetheless, we remain content since the numerical tests in Sect. 4 show that Algorithm 4 is superior to the basic approach and that the penalty parameter consistently remains bounded away from zero.
All together, we believe that these experiments are the best way to isolate and measure the performance of our adaptive penalty parameter updating procedure.
